platforms.title: Prediabetes Result? Extra Weight Might Be Behind It
platforms.meta_description: Told you have prediabetes? NIDDK says it can be reversed. Losing 5 to 7% of your weight and moving 150 minutes a week cut new diabetes by 58% in the DPP trial.
platforms.body_html:
The lab report shows an A1C or a fasting glucose that is a little too high. Your doctor uses the word prediabetes, mentions diet and exercise, and the appointment is over. It is easy to walk out thinking this is just the slow start of type 2 diabetes. It does not have to be. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) says plainly that you can take steps to prevent or reverse your prediabetes. The open question is what those steps are, and how big they need to be.

What the Prediabetes Numbers Mean

According to NIDDK, you have prediabetes if your A1C is between 5.7% and 6.4%, or if your fasting plasma glucose is between 100 and 125 mg/dL. An oral glucose tolerance test, which measures your blood sugar two hours after a sweet drink, points to prediabetes at 140 to 199 mg/dL, though NIDDK notes it is used less often because it takes longer and costs more. These ranges come from the American Diabetes Association; the World Health Organization and several European countries draw the fasting line at 110 mg/dL instead, so a friend abroad may hear a different cut-off for the same result.

Why act now rather than later? NIDDK says people with prediabetes have a high chance of developing type 2 diabetes within 5 to 10 years. Most people feel nothing at this stage, which is exactly why the number on paper matters. NIDDK says your health care professional may order tests if you are 35 or older, or if you have overweight or obesity plus other risk factors such as a family history of diabetes. Once prediabetes is found, NIDDK says you should be tested for type 2 diabetes every year.

Why Extra Weight Pushes Blood Sugar Up

Insulin is the hormone that moves glucose out of your blood and into muscle, fat and liver cells. NIDDK describes insulin resistance as a state in which the body no longer responds to insulin the way it should. The pancreas tries to keep up by making more insulin. For a while that works, and glucose stays near normal. Over time it falls behind, and glucose starts to drift into the prediabetes range.

NIDDK lists having overweight, obesity or a large waist size among the risk factors, along with physical inactivity, age and family history. You cannot change your age or your relatives. You can change the two factors that feed insulin resistance most directly: how much extra weight you carry and how much your muscles are asked to work. Working muscles pull glucose out of the blood, and that is a large part of why activity helps even before the scale moves.

So What Actually Reverses It?

The clearest answer comes from the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), an NIH-funded randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2002. It enrolled 3,234 adults with raised fasting and after-meal glucose and followed them for an average of 2.8 years. In that trial, the lifestyle group aimed for at least a 7% weight loss and at least 150 minutes of physical activity a week. Compared with placebo, the DPP lifestyle program reduced new cases of diabetes by 58%, while the drug metformin reduced them by 31%.

NIDDK turns that study into a practical target: losing 5% to 7% of your starting weight helped people at high risk lower their chance of developing diabetes. For someone weighing 200 pounds, that is 10 to 14 pounds, not a total body makeover. The 150 minutes can be split into about 30 minutes of brisk walking on five days. NIDDK also lists healthy foods and drinks, enough sleep and, in some cases, metformin or weight-loss medicine prescribed by a health care professional.

Does getting back to normal glucose actually matter if it does not last? A follow-up analysis of DPP participants, published in the Lancet in 2012, found that people who returned to normal glucose regulation at least once during the trial had a 56% lower risk of later diabetes than those who stayed in the prediabetes range. That is an observational finding, so it shows an association rather than proof, but it suggests each return to normal is worth chasing.

Where to Start This Week

Use NIDDK's calculator or a phone calculator to work out 5% of your weight and write that number down. Pick three or four days for a 30-minute walk and put them in your calendar like appointments. Then ask about the National Diabetes Prevention Program, the lifestyle change program NIDDK points to, which gives you structure and support rather than a leaflet.

Quick recap before you close this page:

  • Your range: fasting glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL or A1C 5.7% to 6.4% means prediabetes in the US system.
  • Your weight goal: the 5% to 7% of today's weight that NIDDK cites from the DPP.
  • Your activity goal: 150 minutes a week, the DPP target.
  • Your follow-up: the yearly test NIDDK recommends, on a date you have actually booked.

This article is general information and does not replace advice from your own doctor.

Sources: NIDDK, "Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes" (last reviewed March 2025); Knowler WC et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2002; Perreault L et al., Lancet, 2012.
